The task in Q5 invited students to write a speech for their school or college peers to argue their point of view on the idea that happiness and success are the result of determination and hard work rather than luck or where we are from. This gave students six relatively abstract ideas to play with in their answers. Students appeared to understand and engage well with all these concepts.

There are some genuine positives to report in terms of structuring arguments; sequencing of ideas; incorporating introductions and conclusions; offering a range of appropriate rhetorical devices and adapting tone and style to suit audience and purpose. This was particularly noticeable as students were routinely able to channel the many assemblies and tutorial sessions they had attended and repeat many of the remonstrations and pleading of their teachers to work harder and show their grit and determination in school or college. These were all strengths which were very satisfying to note.

Where students struggled was in generating ideas and developing those ideas into coherent, connected points of view. The task offered students, if they chose, the opportunity to explore their own definitions of concepts such as happiness or luck, and many did precisely that. There was, as always, the chance to agree or disagree with the statement. Although the majority chose to agree with the statement and presented homilies on the value of hard work, others took a different approach and explored the inequalities in society which mean that some start well ahead of others in the race of life, often asking the audience to compare the lives of two very different students and their learning environments. On this occasion, students who disagreed tended to find a richer vein of ideas to develop than those who simply agreed. This is not always the case. As has been stated before in this report, but it is worth repeating - general, abstract ideas are encouraged in the writing task, but they need to be substantiated by specific examples and granular explanation. The reverse is also true: personal anecdotes and experience are also welcome but need to be expanded to take in the bigger picture and the big ideas.

Common strengths

The best responses were those where the student presented a coherent response to the statement which included some clear ideas about the concepts of happiness and success. Many offered suggestions about the power of generational wealth; the influence of having celebrity parents or the impact of private education on the life chances of a student. They were able to provide concrete examples of where young people had bucked the trend of their working-class peers to succeed against the odds, or conversely to bemoan the impossibility of achieving success when politics and society were stacked against you from the start. Students working at Level 3 developed their ideas within paragraphs, clearly explaining what lessons were learnt, how we have benefited from learning about them and how we should continue to appreciate their sacrifice. These clear connected ideas were expressed using a range of vocabulary clearly chosen for effect, with a scattering of linguistic devices used to engage their readers. Technically, responses at Level 3 were characterised by the word ‘mostly’ in that their range of punctuation, sentence control and spelling were mostly accurate, with a variety of sentence forms deployed for impact.

The very best responses were, as expected, few and far between in the November series, but there were some examples of compelling arguments. Students working at Level 4 were able to offer an original perspective, such as that of the student hoping to be an actor and finding that the progeny of celebrities are several rungs above her on the staircase to fame, criticising the instant notoriety of the Kardashians, for example – famous only for being famous – who have never done a hard day’s work in their lives and trade on nothing more than their charisma on the fast track to success. The tone and style of these Level 4 responses are typically characterised by a sense of confidence, conviction and consistency. These responses tend to be detailed and offer more complex ideas, reflecting the critical thinking and conscious crafting of the students. Technically, these responses are not without error but demonstrate either an ambitious range of skill or a higher level of accuracy. Students working at Level 4 are likely to be evidencing a confident and assured control of a range of more complex grammatical structures and a wider and more diverse range of punctuation, along with a more ambitious vocabulary which enables them to demonstrate the most complex and accurate spellings. However, the separation of the content and accuracy marks allows examiners to reward students for the quality of their ideas, regardless of the technical inaccuracies, as the AO6 mark is a completely independent judgement. Common misunderstandings

In Level 1 responses, students typically took the six ideas in the statement and offered them back to the audience in the same or a different order. This over-dependence on the ideas in the statement meant that they provided only very simple ideas of their own and were often unable to demonstrate any variety in their own vocabulary. Level 1 responses tended to be brief and under-developed, with few attempts to sequence or link ideas or to structure their speech into paragraphs. There were occasional linguistic devices used and where they were deployed, students tended to demonstrate some technical skill too, in varying their sentence forms or increasing their range of punctuation.

At Level 2, students typically offered generalised responses; those who were able to offer a more interesting variety of relevant ideas were likely to be rewarded at the upper end of the level. Some students focused their answer on the importance of hard work and determination and tried to explain how these are linked to happiness and success without much sense of what they understood by those terms. Success was frequently assumed to be financial or professional and happiness was often tacked on as an additional benefit of either/both, without exploring the possibility that happiness could stem from any other aspect of life. At the lower end of Level 2, there was little offered other than repeated exhortations that the audience should work harder and be more determined because they could achieve anything. Without the addition of concrete examples and ideas to support these assertions, students struggled to move into Upper Level 2 or indeed into Level 3. There was some evidence at Level 2 of an intent to demonstrate variety of sentence structures and, as a consequence, of punctuation too, which is often the result of the use of a range of linguistic devices and is something worth encouraging students to consider as it provides dual benefits, for both AO5 and AO6. Poor control of agreement continues to be an issue, particularly for those students working in a second or third language. This is clearly an area for improvement but not one which is easy to target in the short space of time between the start of term and the November exam.
